questions.question: What is the COALESCE function used for?
questions.answer: It evaluates arguments sequentially and returns the first non-NULL value in the list.

questions.question: Name three common SQL Server aggregate functions.
questions.answer: COUNT(), SUM(), and AVG().

topics.title: Subqueries & CTEs (Common Table Expressions)
topics.html:
Subqueries & CTEs (Common Table Expressions)

Course: SQL Server

Simplify complex queries using nested subqueries, Correlated Subqueries, and Common Table Expressions (CTEs).

💡 Key Concepts

  • Subquery: A query nested inside another query (e.g. in the WHERE clause).
  • CTE (WITH): A temporary named result set defined within the execution scope of a single query.
  • Correlated Subquery: A nested query that references columns from the outer query, running once per row.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
WITH Sales_CTE AS (
    SELECT SalesPersonId, SUM(Amount) AS TotalSales
    FROM Sales
    GROUP BY SalesPersonId
)
SELECT * FROM Sales_CTE WHERE TotalSales > 50000;

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Using deeply nested subqueries instead of CTEs, which makes SQL code hard to read and maintain.

questions.question: What is a Common Table Expression (CTE)?
questions.answer: A temporary named result set that can be referenced within a SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE statement.

questions.question: What is a correlated subquery?
questions.answer: A subquery that depends on columns from the outer query and is executed once for each row processed by the outer query.

topics.title: Stored Procedures & User Defined Functions
topics.html:
Stored Procedures & User Defined Functions

Course: SQL Server

Encapsulate SQL logic into reusable databases assets: Stored Procedures and User Defined Functions (UDFs).

💡 Key Concepts

  • Stored Procedure: Precompiled SQL code block. Can return multiple datasets, modify data, and take parameters.
  • User Defined Function (UDF): Calculates and returns a single scalar value or a table. Cannot modify data.
  • Execution Plan Caching: Procedures compile once and cache plans for faster subsequent executions.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
CREATE PROCEDURE GetEmployeeById @EmpId INT
AS
BEGIN
    SELECT * FROM Employees WHERE Id = @EmpId;
END;

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Using scalar User Defined Functions inside SELECT lists on large tables, which causes SQL Server to execute the function row-by-row (RBAR - Row By Agonizing Row) and ruins performance.

questions.question: What is the main difference between a Stored Procedure and a Function?
questions.answer: Procedures can modify database tables and execute transactions. Functions cannot modify state and must return a value.

questions.question: What is parameter sniffing?
questions.answer: A compilation behavior where SQL Server compiles a procedure plan using the parameters passed on the first run, which can be inefficient for other parameter values.

topics.title: Views & Triggers
topics.html:
Views & Triggers

Course: SQL Server

Create virtual tables using Views, and intercept database actions (Insert, Update, Delete) using Triggers.

💡 Key Concepts

  • View: A virtual table based on a SELECT query. Simplifies security and complex queries.
  • DML Triggers: Code executed automatically when data in a table is modified.
  • Inserted & Deleted Tables: Temporary tables accessible inside triggers containing row state modifications.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
CREATE VIEW ActiveEmployees AS
SELECT Id, Name FROM Employees WHERE IsActive = 1;

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Overusing Triggers to manage business logic, which makes debugging extremely difficult because code runs invisibly.

questions.question: What are the Inserted and Deleted tables in triggers?
questions.answer: Temporary, memory-resident tables containing the state of rows before and after the modification.

questions.question: Does a view store data physically?
questions.answer: No, standard views are virtual tables. Indexed views (materialized views), however, do store data physically on disk.

topics.title: ACID Properties & Transactions
topics.html:
ACID Properties & Transactions

Course: SQL Server

Ensure database integrity using transactions that satisfy ACID properties: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability.

💡 Key Concepts

  • Atomicity: Ensures all database actions in a transaction succeed, or all roll back (All-or-Nothing).
  • Consistency: Guarantees the database transitions from one valid state to another.
  • Isolation / Durability: Isolation keeps concurrent transactions separate. Durability ensures committed changes survive crashes.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
BEGIN TRANSACTION;
BEGIN TRY
    UPDATE Accounts SET Balance -= 100 WHERE Id = 1;
    UPDATE Accounts SET Balance += 100 WHERE Id = 2;
    COMMIT TRANSACTION;
END TRY
BEGIN CATCH
    ROLLBACK TRANSACTION;
END CATCH;

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Leaving transactions open by forgetting COMMIT or ROLLBACK, which blocks locks and causes database freezes.

questions.question: What does ACID stand for?
questions.answer: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability, the core principles of reliable database transactions.

questions.question: What happens if a SQL query fails inside a BEGIN TRANSACTION block without error handling?
questions.answer: The transaction remains open and lock resources stay blocked until the connection is closed or rolled back.

topics.title: Transaction Isolation Levels
topics.html:
Transaction Isolation Levels

Course: SQL Server

Control database locks behavior and prevent anomalies like Dirty Reads, Non-Repeatable Reads, and Phantom Reads.

💡 Key Concepts

  • Read Uncommitted: Allows reading uncommitted data, causing Dirty Reads. Low lock overhead.
  • Read Committed: Default level. Prevents dirty reads by holding shared locks until reads finish.
  • Serializable: Highest isolation. Places range locks to prevent phantom reads.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SNAPSHOT;
BEGIN TRANSACTION;
SELECT * FROM Products;
COMMIT TRANSACTION;

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Setting isolation level to Serializable unnecessarily, which blocks concurrent queries and slows down execution.

questions.question: What is a dirty read?
questions.answer: Reading data that has been modified by an active transaction but has not yet been committed.

questions.question: How does Snapshot isolation prevent locking readers?
questions.answer: It uses row versioning in tempdb to show readers the data state at the start of the transaction, avoiding shared locks.

topics.title: Indexing Strategies & Query Optimization
topics.html:
Indexing Strategies & Query Optimization

Course: SQL Server

Optimize database tables using Clustered and Non-Clustered indexes, and analyze execution plans.

💡 Key Concepts

  • Clustered Index: Re-orders table data physically on disk. Only 1 per table.
  • Non-Clustered Index: A separate search index pointing to row IDs. Multiple allowed.
  • Covering Index: Adding INCLUDE columns to indexes so queries resolve entirely within the index.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
CREATE CLUSTERED INDEX IX_Employees_Id ON Employees(Id);
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_Employees_Email ON Employees(Email) INCLUDE(Name);

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Adding indexes to every column, which slows down INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE queries because all indexes must be rebuilt.

questions.question: What is a covering index?
questions.answer: An index that contains all the columns referenced by a query, allowing results to resolve without table lookups.

questions.question: What is the difference between an Index Scan and an Index Seek?
questions.answer: A scan searches the entire index tree (slow). A seek navigates directly to matching rows using search keys (fast).

topics.title: Database Normalization
topics.html:
Database Normalization

Course: SQL Server

Minimize data redundancy and prevent anomalies by normalizing tables into 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, and BCNF.

💡 Key Concepts

  • 1NF (First Normal Form): Atomic columns and unique rows. No repeating groups.
  • 2NF (Second Normal Form): Meets 1NF. Removes partial dependencies (all columns depend on the entire primary key).
  • 3NF (Third Normal Form): Meets 2NF. Removes transitive dependencies (non-key columns depend only on the primary key).

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
// 3NF Rule: ZipCode table should hold City/State columns,
// and Customers table should only store ZipCodeId.

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Over-normalizing simple databases, which requires joining too many tables for basic queries and slows down performance.

questions.question: What is transitive dependency in 3NF?
questions.answer: When a non-key column depends on another non-key column, rather than directly on the primary key.

questions.question: When is denormalization acceptable?
questions.answer: In read-heavy reporting systems (Data Warehouses) to reduce JOIN complexity and speed up reads.

topics.title: SQL Server Security Policies
topics.html:
SQL Server Security Policies

Course: SQL Server

Secure database instances using logins, users, schemas, and Row-Level Security (RLS).

💡 Key Concepts

  • Logins vs Users: Logins grant server connection access. Users grant access to specific databases.
  • Row-Level Security (RLS): Filters query rows automatically based on user roles and security predicates.
  • SQL Injection Prevention: Always use parameterized queries, never concatenate SQL strings.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
CREATE SECURITY POLICY SalesFilter
ADD FILTRATION PREDICATE dbo.fn_securitypredicate(SalesPersonId)
ON dbo.Orders;

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Using the "sa" (system administrator) account for application connections, exposing full database access.

questions.question: What is the difference between a Login and a User?
questions.answer: A Login is for server authentication. A User is database-specific, mapping a login to table access.

questions.question: How do parameterized queries prevent SQL injection?
questions.answer: By treating inputs strictly as literal values rather than executable SQL commands.

topics.title: Disaster Recovery (Backup & Restore)
topics.html:
Disaster Recovery (Backup & Restore)

Course: SQL Server

Plan database recovery strategies using Full, Differential, and Transaction Log backups.

💡 Key Concepts

  • Backup Types: Full (entire DB), Differential (changes since last Full), Log (changes since last Log backup).
  • Recovery Models: Simple (no log backups, auto-truncates), Full (retains transaction logs, allows point-in-time recovery).
  • Point-In-Time Restore: Restoring a database to a specific second before a corruption event.

💻 Practical Code Example

C# / CODE BLOCK
BACKUP DATABASE TutorialDb TO DISK = 'D:\Backup\TutorialDb.bak';
BACKUP LOG TutorialDb TO DISK = 'D:\Backup\TutorialDb_Log.trn';

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Mistakes

Running database recovery in Full Recovery Model without setting up Transaction Log backups, causing transaction log files (.ldf) to grow until the disk is full.

questions.question: Why does the transaction log grow continuously in Full Recovery Model?
questions.answer: Because SQL Server keeps the log until a Transaction Log backup is run to truncate committed logs.

questions.question: What is a differential backup?
questions.answer: A backup that contains all changes made to the database since the last full database backup.

topics.title: React
topics.html:
Section 1: React Fundamentals

1. Tell me about React.

React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces developed by Meta. It follows a component-based architecture, which allows us to build reusable UI components and compose them together to create complex applications.

One of React's key strengths is its Virtual DOM, which helps optimize rendering performance by updating only the parts of the UI that have changed.

In my projects, I primarily use React for building Single Page Applications where maintainability, reusability, and performance are important. I typically combine React with APIs, state management solutions like Context API or Redux Toolkit, and routing libraries such as React Router.

Real Project Example

In my project, I created reusable components such as DataTable, SearchBar, Pagination, and Modal. These components were reused across multiple screens, reducing duplicate code and making maintenance easier.

Follow-up Questions

Q: Why choose React over Angular?

React gives more flexibility because it's a library rather than a complete framework. We can choose our own routing, state management, and architecture based on project needs.

Q: Why choose React over Vanilla JavaScript?

React provides component reusability, state management, efficient rendering, and a structured way to build large applications.

2. What is JSX?

JSX stands for JavaScript XML. It allows us to write HTML-like syntax inside JavaScript code.

Although JSX looks like HTML, browsers don't understand it directly. During the build process, Babel converts JSX into React.createElement() function calls.

JSX improves readability and developer productivity because UI structure and logic can be written together.

Example

const element = <h1>Hello React</h1>;

Internally:

React.createElement(

 "h1",

 null,

 "Hello React"

);

Follow-up Question

Why use className instead of class?

Because class is a reserved keyword in JavaScript, React uses className instead.

3. What is the Virtual DOM?

The Virtual DOM is a lightweight JavaScript representation of the actual DOM.

Whenever state or props change, React creates a new Virtual DOM tree and compares it with the previous Virtual DOM tree.

React then determines exactly what changed and updates only those specific elements in the real DOM.

Since DOM operations are expensive, this approach significantly improves performance.

Real Example

Imagine a page with:

100 Products

If only Product 25 changes:

Without React:

  • Entire UI may re-render

With React:

  • Only Product 25 gets updated

Follow-up Question

Does React directly update the DOM?

No. React first updates the Virtual DOM and then updates only the required parts of the real DOM.

4. What is Reconciliation?

Reconciliation is React's algorithm for comparing the previous Virtual DOM tree with the new Virtual DOM tree.

The purpose is to determine the minimum number of changes required in the real DOM.

This process is often called Diffing.

Interview Shortcut

Virtual DOM creates snapshots.

Reconciliation compares snapshots.

React updates only what's different.

Common Follow-up

Difference between Virtual DOM and Reconciliation?

Virtual DOM is the data structure.

Reconciliation is the process used to compare Virtual DOM trees.

5. What are Components in React?

Components are reusable building blocks of a React application.

Each component contains its own UI and logic.

By breaking an application into components, we improve maintainability, reusability, and testability.

Example

App

├ Navbar

├ Sidebar

├ ProductList

└ Footer

Real Project Example

Instead of creating separate tables everywhere, I usually build a reusable DataTable component and pass configuration through props.

6. Functional Components vs Class Components

Functional components are JavaScript functions that return JSX.

Class components are ES6 classes that extend React.Component.

Today, functional components are preferred because Hooks provide state management and lifecycle capabilities without requiring classes.

Functional Component

function User() {

 return <h1>User</h1>;

}

Class Component

class User extends React.Component {

 render() {

   return <h1>User</h1>;

 }

}

Which One Do You Use?

In modern React development, I use functional components almost exclusively because they are simpler, cleaner, and fully support Hooks.

7. What are Props?

Props are inputs passed from a parent component to a child component.

They allow components to be reusable and configurable.

Props are read-only, meaning child components should never modify them.

Example

<User name="Ashutosh" />

function User(props) {

 return <h1>{props.name}</h1>;

}

Follow-up

Can props be modified?

No. Props are immutable. If data needs to change, state should be used.

8. What is State?

State represents data managed within a component.

Unlike props, state can change over time.

When state changes, React automatically re-renders the component.

Example

const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

Difference Between Props and State

Props

State

Passed from parent

Managed internally

Read-only

Can change

External data

Internal data

9. Why Should State Not Be Updated Directly?

Bad:

count = count + 1;

Good:

setCount(count + 1);

React tracks updates through state setter functions.

Directly modifying state bypasses React's rendering system and can cause UI inconsistencies.

Follow-up

Why does React need setState/useState setter?

React uses those functions to schedule updates and trigger re-renders efficiently.

10. What are Keys in React?

Keys help React uniquely identify elements inside lists.

During reconciliation, React uses keys to determine which elements were added, removed, or updated.

Example

users.map(user => (

 <User

   key={user.id}

   user={user}

 />

))

Common Mistake

key={index}

Why Avoid Index?

If list order changes, React may incorrectly reuse components, causing rendering bugs and performance issues.

Section 2: Hooks Deep Dive

11. What is useState?

useState is a React Hook that allows functional components to manage state.

Before Hooks were introduced, state management was only possible in class components. useState made it possible to manage state directly inside functional components.

It returns an array containing the current state value and a function to update that state.

Example

const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

Real Project Example

In a search screen, I use useState to manage search text, loading states, selected filters, and API results.

Follow-up Questions

Q: Does updating state immediately update the value?

No. State updates are asynchronous. React schedules the update and re-renders the component.

Q: How do you update state based on previous state?

setCount(prev => prev + 1);

This avoids stale state issues.

12. What is useEffect?

useEffect is used to handle side effects in React components.

Side effects include API calls, subscriptions, timers, event listeners, logging, or any operation outside React's rendering process.

It allows us to perform actions after the component renders.

Example

useEffect(() => {

 fetchUsers();

}, []);

Real Project Example

Whenever a page loads, I use useEffect to call backend APIs and populate the UI.

Follow-up Questions

Q: When does useEffect run?

By default, after every render unless controlled by dependencies.

Q: Can we make API calls inside useEffect?

Yes, that's one of its most common use cases.

13. Dependency Array in useEffect

The dependency array controls when useEffect executes.

Case 1: No Dependency Array

useEffect(() => {

 console.log("Runs every render");

});

Runs after every render.

Case 2: Empty Dependency Array

useEffect(() => {

 fetchData();

}, []);

Runs only once when the component mounts.

Case 3: With Dependencies

useEffect(() => {

 searchUsers();

}, [searchTerm]);

Runs whenever searchTerm changes.

Interview Tip

Understanding dependency arrays is critical because most React bugs involving useEffect come from incorrect dependencies.

14. What is the Cleanup Function?

Cleanup functions prevent memory leaks by removing resources when a component unmounts or before the effect runs again.

Example

useEffect(() => {

 const timer = setInterval(() => {

   console.log("Running");

 }, 1000);

 return () => clearInterval(timer);

}, []);

Real Project Example

When listening for browser resize events, I remove the listener in cleanup to prevent memory leaks.

Follow-up Question

Why is cleanup important?

Without cleanup, unnecessary subscriptions, timers, or event listeners remain active even after the component is removed.

15. What Causes Infinite Loops in useEffect?

Infinite loops happen when an effect updates state that is also listed as a dependency.

Example

useEffect(() => {

 setCount(count + 1);

}, [count]);

What Happens?

count changes

↓

effect runs

↓

state updates

↓

re-render

↓

effect runs again

Infinite cycle.

Solution

Review dependencies carefully and avoid unnecessary state updates inside effects.

Interview Tip

Infinite loop questions are extremely common in React interviews.

16. What is useRef?

useRef provides a mutable object whose value persists across renders without causing re-renders.

It is commonly used for DOM access and storing mutable values.

Example

const inputRef = useRef();

inputRef.current.focus();

Real Project Example

After opening a modal, I automatically focus the first input field using useRef.

Follow-up Questions

Q: Does updating useRef trigger re-render?

No.

Q: Difference between useRef and useState?

useState triggers re-renders, useRef does not.

17. What is useMemo?

useMemo is a performance optimization hook that memoizes expensive calculations.

It prevents recalculating values when dependencies haven't changed.

Example

const total = useMemo(() => {

 return calculateTotal(products);

}, [products]);

Real Project Example

In reporting dashboards, I use useMemo to calculate totals and aggregates for large datasets.

Follow-up Questions

Q: Should useMemo be used everywhere?

No. It also has overhead. Use it only for expensive computations.

Q: Is useMemo guaranteed optimization?

No. It's a performance hint, not a guarantee.

18. What is useCallback?

useCallback memoizes functions so that React doesn't create a new function instance on every render.

Example

const handleClick = useCallback(() => {

 console.log("clicked");

}, []);

Real Project Example

When passing event handlers to child components wrapped with React.memo, I use useCallback to prevent unnecessary re-renders.

Follow-up Questions

Q: Why not just define functions normally?

A new function gets created on every render, which may trigger child component re-renders.

19. useMemo vs useCallback

Both are optimization hooks.

useMemo

Returns a value.

const total = useMemo(() => {

 return calculateTotal(items);

}, [items]);

useCallback

Returns a function.

const handleClick = useCallback(() => {

}, []);

Interview Shortcut

useMemo caches results.

useCallback caches functions.

20. What is useReducer?

useReducer is a Hook used for complex state management.

Instead of multiple useState calls, state transitions are handled through actions and reducers.

Example

const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(

 reducer,

 initialState

);

Why Use It?

When state logic becomes complicated:

Add User

Delete User

Update User

Reset User

Managing everything with useState becomes messy.

Real Project Example

I use useReducer for forms with many fields and complex validation logic.

21. When Would You Choose useReducer Over useState?

Use useState for:

Simple state

Counter

Input field

Modal open/close

Use useReducer for:

Complex state transitions

Large forms

Multiple related states

Business workflows

Interview One-Liner

useState is simpler; useReducer provides better structure for complex state logic.

22. What is useContext?

useContext allows components to consume values from React Context without manually passing props through every level.

Problem Solved

Without Context:

App

↓

Parent

↓

Child

↓

GrandChild

Passing user information through every component.

With Context:

Context Provider

↓

Any Component

Direct access.

Real Project Example

I use Context for authenticated user information, themes, and application settings.

23. What are Custom Hooks?

Custom Hooks are reusable JavaScript functions that internally use React Hooks.

They help share logic across multiple components.

Example

function useUsers() {

 const [users, setUsers] = useState([]);

 useEffect(() => {

   fetchUsers();

 }, []);

 return users;

}

Real Project Example

Instead of repeating API fetching logic across screens, I create custom hooks like:

  • useUsers()
  • useProducts()
  • useAuth()

Follow-up Question

Why use Custom Hooks?

To improve code reuse and maintainability.

24. What is useLayoutEffect?

useLayoutEffect is similar to useEffect but runs synchronously before the browser paints the screen.

Sequence

Render

↓

useLayoutEffect

↓

Paint

useEffect

Render

↓

Paint

↓

useEffect

Real Project Example

When calculating element dimensions before rendering, I use useLayoutEffect to avoid visual flickering.

Interview Tip

Most applications only need useEffect.

25. What is forwardRef?

forwardRef allows parent components to access a child component's DOM element.

Example

const Input = forwardRef((props, ref) => {

 return <input ref={ref} />;

});

Parent:

const inputRef = useRef();

Real Project Example

I use forwardRef in reusable form components where parent components need access to focus or validation methods.

26. What is useImperativeHandle?

useImperativeHandle customizes what a parent component can access through a ref.

Example

useImperativeHandle(ref, () => ({

 focusInput() {

   inputRef.current.focus();

 }

}));

Why Use It?

Instead of exposing the entire child component, expose only specific methods.

Real Project Example

I use it in reusable modal and form components where parent components need controlled access.

27. What are the Rules of Hooks?

React Hooks follow two important rules:

Rule 1

Only call Hooks at the top level.

❌ Wrong

if (loggedIn) {

 useEffect(() => {});

}

✅ Correct

useEffect(() => {

 if (loggedIn) {

   // logic

 }

}, [loggedIn]);

Rule 2

Only call Hooks from:

  • Functional Components
  • Custom Hooks

❌ Wrong

function fetchUsers() {

 useState();

}

Why?

React relies on consistent Hook execution order.

Interview One-Liner

Hooks must always execute in the same order on every render.

Most Asked Hooks Interview Questions (Deep Dive Answers)

These are the answers I'd actually recommend giving in an interview rather than textbook definitions.

28. Explain useEffect Lifecycle

In functional components, useEffect is used to handle lifecycle-related operations.

It can simulate componentDidMount, componentDidUpdate, and componentWillUnmount from class components.

Depending on the dependency array, useEffect behaves differently.

Mount Phase

useEffect(() => {

 console.log("Mounted");

}, []);

Runs once when the component loads.

Equivalent to:

componentDidMount()

Update Phase

useEffect(() => {

 console.log("Search changed");

}, [searchTerm]);

Runs whenever searchTerm changes.

Equivalent to:

componentDidUpdate()

Unmount Phase

useEffect(() => {

 return () => {

   console.log("Cleanup");

 };

}, []);

Runs when component is removed.

Equivalent to:

componentWillUnmount()

Real Project Example

On a User Management page, I use useEffect to load users during mount, refresh data when filters change, and remove subscriptions during unmount.

Follow-up Question

Can useEffect replace all lifecycle methods?

Almost all common lifecycle functionality can be handled using useEffect.

29. Difference Between useEffect and useLayoutEffect

Both hooks execute side effects, but the timing is different.

useEffect

Render

↓

Browser Paint

↓

useEffect

Runs after UI becomes visible.

useLayoutEffect

Render

↓

useLayoutEffect

↓

Browser Paint

Runs before the browser paints.

Example Use Case

Suppose we need to measure element width.

useLayoutEffect(() => {

 console.log(divRef.current.offsetWidth);

}, []);

Using useEffect may cause flickering because rendering happens first.

Real Project Example

I rarely use useLayoutEffect. Most business applications only require useEffect. I use useLayoutEffect when DOM measurements must happen before the user sees the page.

Interview Tip

If you are unsure, use useEffect. useLayoutEffect is for special DOM-related scenarios.

30. What Causes Infinite Loops in useEffect?

Infinite loops happen when useEffect continuously updates a dependency that causes itself to run again.

Example

useEffect(() => {

 setCount(count + 1);

}, [count]);

Process:

count changes

↓

effect runs

↓

setCount

↓

re-render

↓

effect runs again

Loop forever.

Common Causes

State Update Inside Effect

useEffect(() => {

 setData(newData);

}, [data]);

Function Dependencies

const fetchData = () => {};

useEffect(() => {

 fetchData();

}, [fetchData]);

New function gets created every render.

Solution

const fetchData = useCallback(() => {}, []);

Interview Tip

Most useEffect bugs come from incorrect dependencies.

31. useRef vs useState

Both store values, but behave differently.

useState

useRef

Triggers re-render

Does not trigger re-render

Used for UI state

Used for mutable values

React tracks changes

React ignores changes

Example

useState

const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

Updating count re-renders UI.

useRef

const countRef = useRef(0);

Updating:

countRef.current++;

No re-render occurs.

Real Project Example

I use:

useState

  • Form fields
  • Search values
  • API results

useRef

  • Input focus
  • Timers
  • Previous values
  • DOM references

Interview Question

Can useRef replace useState?

No. Since useRef doesn't trigger rendering, UI won't update automatically.

32. useMemo vs useCallback

Both are optimization hooks but solve different problems.

useMemo

Caches a value.

const total = useMemo(() => {

 return calculateTotal(products);

}, [products]);

Returns:

5000

useCallback

Caches a function.

const handleClick = useCallback(() => {

 console.log("clicked");

}, []);

Returns:

function reference

Interview Shortcut

useMemo memoizes results.

useCallback memoizes functions.

Real Project Example

I use:

useMemo

  • Dashboard calculations
  • Report totals
  • Filtering large datasets

useCallback

  • Event handlers passed to child components

Follow-up Question

Can useCallback be implemented using useMemo?

Yes.

useMemo(() => fn, deps);

Internally, useCallback behaves similarly.

33. When Should You Use useReducer?

useReducer is useful when state logic becomes complex and multiple state updates depend on actions.

Simple State

const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

Good candidate for useState.

Complex State

Add User

Delete User

Update User

Reset User

Search User

Better candidate for useReducer.

Example

const [state, dispatch] =

 useReducer(reducer, initialState);

Real Project Example

I use useReducer in large forms where validation, submission, reset, and field updates all affect related state.

Interview Tip

If state transitions resemble business actions, useReducer is usually a good fit.

34. Context API vs Redux

Both solve global state management but differ in scale.

Context API

Good for:

Theme

User Info

Language

Permissions

Advantages:

  • Built into React
  • Easy setup
  • No external library

Redux Toolkit

Good for:

Large enterprise apps

Complex workflows

Shared business state

Advantages:

  • Predictable state
  • Middleware
  • DevTools
  • Better scalability

Real Project Answer

For simple global data such as authentication or themes, I prefer Context API.

For applications with multiple modules and complex state interactions, I prefer Redux Toolkit.

Interview Question

Can Context replace Redux?

For small applications yes. For large enterprise applications Redux usually scales better.

35. Advantages of Custom Hooks

Custom Hooks allow us to reuse stateful logic across components.

Without Custom Hook

useEffect(() => {

 fetchUsers();

}, []);

Repeated in multiple components.

With Custom Hook

const users = useUsers();

Logic centralized.

Benefits

Reusability

Write once.

Use everywhere.

Cleaner Components

Components focus on UI.

Hook handles logic.

Easier Testing

Logic isolated from UI.

Real Project Example

I often create:

useAuth()

useUsers()

useProducts()

usePagination()

useDebounce()

Interview Tip

Custom Hooks improve maintainability and reduce duplicated code.

36. What Are Common use cases of forwardRef?

forwardRef allows parent components to access a child component's DOM element.

Example

Reusable Input Component

const Input = forwardRef((props, ref) => {

 return <input ref={ref} />;

});

Parent:

inputRef.current.focus();

Real Project Use Cases

Auto Focus

inputRef.current.focus();

Form Libraries

Libraries like:

  • React Hook Form
  • Formik

often use refs.

Reusable UI Components

Input

TextArea

Dropdown

DatePicker

Interview Tip

forwardRef is commonly used when building reusable component libraries.

37. What Are Common use cases of useImperativeHandle?

useImperativeHandle allows a child component to expose only specific methods to its parent through refs.

Without useImperativeHandle

Parent gets full access.

ref.current

With useImperativeHandle

Expose only required functionality.

useImperativeHandle(ref, () => ({

 focusInput() {

   inputRef.current.focus();

 }

}));

Real Project Example

Reusable Modal Component

Parent:

modalRef.current.open();

Child:

open()

close()

reset()

Exposed through useImperativeHandle.

Benefits

Better Encapsulation

Parent cannot access everything.

Cleaner APIs

Expose only necessary methods.

Interview Tip

useImperativeHandle is frequently paired with forwardRef when building reusable UI components such as modals, dialogs, forms, and custom inputs.

Senior-Level Hook Questions Interviewers Love

These questions are commonly asked in senior React interviews because they test whether you understand how React works internally, not just how to use Hooks.

38. Why Does useEffect Run Twice in React StrictMode?

In React 18 development mode, StrictMode intentionally runs effects twice to help developers identify side effects that are not properly cleaned up.

This behavior only occurs in development and does not happen in production builds.

Example

useEffect(() => {

 console.log("API Call");

}, []);

In development:

API Call

API Call

May appear twice.

What React Actually Does

Mount

↓

Run Effect

↓

Cleanup

↓

Mount Again

↓

Run Effect Again

React simulates mounting twice.

Why?

React wants to verify:

  • Cleanup functions work correctly
  • Effects are idempotent
  • Memory leaks are prevented

Real Interview Example

If I see duplicate API calls in development, I first check whether StrictMode is enabled before assuming there's a bug.

Follow-up Question

Does this happen in production?

No. Production executes effects normally.

39. How Does React Determine Hook Execution Order?

React identifies Hooks based on the order in which they are called during rendering.

React does not use Hook names.

It relies entirely on call order.

Example

function User() {

 const [name] = useState("");

 const [age] = useState(0);

 return null;

}

React internally sees:

Hook #1 → name

Hook #2 → age

Next Render

React expects:

Hook #1 → name

Hook #2 → age

Again in the same order.

Why Is This Important?

If Hook order changes:

if (loggedIn) {

 useState();

}

React loses track.

Interview Shortcut

React associates state with Hook position, not variable names.

40. Why Shouldn't Hooks Be Called Conditionally?

Hooks must execute in exactly the same order on every render.

Conditional Hooks can change execution order, causing React to associate state with the wrong Hook.

Wrong

if (loggedIn) {

 useEffect(() => {});

}

First Render

Hook #1

Hook #2

Hook #3

Second Render

Hook #1

Hook #3

Order changed.

React becomes confused.

Correct

useEffect(() => {

 if (loggedIn) {

   // logic

 }

}, [loggedIn]);

Interview Tip

Hook calls should be unconditional; conditional logic belongs inside the Hook.

41. How Does React Store Hook State Internally?

Internally, React stores Hook data in a linked list attached to each component's Fiber node.

Every Hook call creates an entry in this internal structure.

Simplified:

Component Fiber

│

├ Hook #1

├ Hook #2

├ Hook #3

└ Hook #4

During Re-render

React walks through:

Hook #1

Hook #2

Hook #3

Hook #4

In sequence.

Why Hook Order Matters

Because React retrieves state by position.

Position 1 → useState

Position 2 → useEffect

Position 3 → useMemo

Interview Tip

This is the technical reason behind the Rules of Hooks.

42. When Can useMemo Hurt Performance?

Many developers think useMemo always improves performance, but it also introduces overhead.

React must store dependencies, compare them, and manage the cached value.

Bad Example

const fullName = useMemo(() => {

 return firstName + lastName;

}, [firstName, lastName]);

Computation is trivial.

No real benefit.

Good Example

const report = useMemo(() => {

 return processLargeDataset(data);

}, [data]);

Expensive calculation.

Significant benefit.

Real Project Example

I use useMemo for large reports, dashboards, filtering, sorting, and aggregation—not simple string concatenation.

useMemo should be used only when the cost of recalculation is greater than the cost of memoization.

43. When Can useCallback Hurt Performance?

Similar to useMemo, useCallback is not free.

React must maintain dependency tracking and store function references.

Bad Example

const handleClick = useCallback(() => {

 console.log("clicked");

}, []);

Used nowhere.

No optimization benefit.

Good Example

const handleClick = useCallback(() => {

 saveUser();

}, [saveUser]);

Passed to:

<Child onClick={handleClick} />

Where Child is wrapped with:

React.memo()

Interview Tip

useCallback only becomes useful when function identity matters.

Common Mistake

Using useCallback everywhere often makes code harder to read without improving performance.

44. How Would You Debug an Infinite useEffect Loop?

I follow a structured approach.

Step 1

Check dependencies.

useEffect(() => {

 setCount(count + 1);

}, [count]);

Immediate red flag.

Step 2

Look for recreated functions.

const fetchUsers = () => {};

Function recreated every render.

Step 3

Check object dependencies.

const filters = {

 active: true

};

New object every render.

Step 4

Use React DevTools.

Inspect:

Render Count

Changed Props

Changed State

Step 5

Add debugging logs.

console.log("Effect Running");

console.log(filters);

Identify what's changing.

Most infinite loops are caused by changing dependencies, recreated functions, or recreated objects.

45. When Should Context API Be Avoided?

Context API is excellent for low-frequency global state but can become inefficient for highly dynamic application state.

Good Use Cases

Theme

Language

Authentication

Permissions

Poor Use Cases

Large Dashboard State

Complex Forms

Frequent Real-Time Updates

Large Enterprise Workflows

Why?

When Context value changes:

Provider

↓

All Consumers Re-render

Potential performance impact.

Better Alternatives

  • Redux Toolkit
  • Zustand
  • Jotai
  • Recoil

Real Project Example

For user authentication I use Context. For business data shared across many modules I prefer Redux Toolkit.

46. Why Doesn't useRef Trigger Re-renders?

React re-renders components when state or props change.

useRef is simply a mutable container.

Example:

const ref = useRef(0);

Update:

ref.current++;

React sees:

Same Ref Object

No re-render.

State Example

setCount(count + 1);

React sees:

State Changed

Triggers render.

Interview Shortcut

useRef updates data, but React does not track those updates for rendering purposes.

Real Use Cases

  • DOM references
  • Timers
  • Previous values
  • Mutable caches

47. Explain React's Hook Rules Internally

React has two official Hook rules:

Rule 1

Only call Hooks at the top level.

Rule 2

Only call Hooks from:

  • Functional Components
  • Custom Hooks

Internal Reason

React stores Hook state based on execution order.

Example:

useState();

useEffect();

useMemo();

React internally maps:

Position 1 → useState

Position 2 → useEffect

Position 3 → useMemo

Next Render

React expects:

Position 1 → useState

Position 2 → useEffect

Position 3 → useMemo

Again.

Problem

if (loggedIn) {

 useEffect();

}

Now Hook positions shift.

Position 1 → useState

Position 2 → useMemo

React loses synchronization.

Interview-Level Explanation

The Rules of Hooks exist because React identifies Hooks by their execution order rather than by names or variables. Consistent ordering allows React to correctly associate state and effects with the appropriate Hook across renders.

Senior Interview Summary (Must Remember)

If an interviewer asks advanced Hook questions, remember these key points:

Hooks Are Order-Based

React tracks Hooks by position, not name.

useEffect Is For Side Effects

API calls, subscriptions, timers, event listeners.

useRef Does Not Trigger Rendering

Because React doesn't track .current changes.

useMemo and useCallback Are Optimizations

Use them only when they solve a real performance problem.

Context Is Not Redux

Context is ideal for simple global state. Redux scales better for complex applications.

StrictMode Double Execution Is Intentional

Development-only behavior to detect unsafe side effects.

Tell me about C#</span></h1><h2 class="c6" id="h.9cfq13iommql"></h2><p class="c1"><span class="c0">C# is a modern, object-oriented, strongly typed programming language developed by Microsoft. It runs on the .NET platform and is widely used for developing web applications, APIs, desktop applications, cloud services, mobile applications, and microservices.</span></p><p class="c1"><span class="c0">One of the key strengths of C# is its support for object-oriented programming principles, type safety, automatic memory management through Garbage Collection, asynchronous programming with async/await, and a rich class library provided by the .NET framework.</span></p><p class="c1"><span class="c0">In my projects, I primarily use C# with ASP.NET Core for developing REST APIs, implementing business logic, integrating with databases through Entity Framework Core, and building scalable backend services.</span></p><hr><p class="c8 c5"><span class="c0"></span></p><h2 class="c6" id="h.ir5151ck7ovz"><span class="c9">Real Project Example</span></h2><p class="c1"><span class="c0">In one of my projects, I used C# and ASP.NET Core to develop a reporting module that processed large amounts of data from SQL Server. I implemented asynchronous programming using async/await to improve application responsiveness and Entity Framework Core for database access.</span></p><p class="c1"><span class="c0">The service exposed REST APIs that were consumed by a React frontend application.</span></p><hr><p class="c8 c5"><span class="c0"></span></p><h2 class="c6" id="h.tfa9qigjro73"><span class="c9">Follow-up Questions</span></h2><h3 class="c4" id="h.kbwc6uvmyv1j"><span class="c12 c10">Q: Why is C# called a strongly typed language?</span></h3><p class="c1"><span class="c0">C# is strongly typed because every variable and object has a defined data type, and the compiler performs type checking at compile time.</span></p><p class="c1"><span class="c0">Example:</span></p><p class="c8"><span class="c7 c2">int age = 25;</span></p><p class="c8"><span class="c7 c2">string name = "Ashutosh";</span></p><p class="c1"><span class="c2"></span><span class="c0">This helps catch errors early and improves code reliability.</span></p><hr><p class="c8 c5"><span class="c0"></span></p><h3 class="c4" id="h.ye1rx4b9k27q"><span class="c12 c10">Q: Is C# compiled or interpreted?</span></h3><p class="c1"><span class="c0">C# is compiled into Intermediate Language (IL) by the compiler. At runtime, the Common Language Runtime (CLR) uses Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation to convert IL into native machine code.</span></p><hr><p class="c8 c5"><span class="c0"></span></p><h3 class="c4" Advanced C#

  1. Task vs Thread
  2. Async/Await Deep Dive
  3. ThreadPool
  4. Parallel Programming
  5. CancellationToken
  6. ConfigureAwait

20. Task vs Thread

A Thread is the smallest unit of execution managed by the operating system, while a Task is a higher-level abstraction introduced in .NET to simplify asynchronous and parallel programming.

A Task typically runs on a ThreadPool thread and provides features such as cancellation, continuation, exception handling, and result management.

In modern .NET applications, I generally use Tasks instead of manually creating Threads because Tasks are more efficient, scalable, and easier to manage.

Real Project Example

Suppose an API needs to generate a report.

Using Thread

Thread thread = new Thread(() =>

{

   GenerateReport();

});

thread.Start();



Using Task

Task.Run(() =>

{

   GenerateReport();

});

The Task approach is preferred because .NET manages thread allocation efficiently through the ThreadPool.

Follow-up Questions

Q: What is a Thread?

A Thread is an actual OS-level execution unit.

Each Thread has:

  • Its own stack
  • Execution context
  • Scheduling overhead

Q: What is a Task?

A Task represents an asynchronous operation.

A Task may use:

ThreadPool Thread

Background Thread

I/O Completion Port

depending on the operation.

Q: Which is preferred in modern .NET?

Task

Because:

  • Easier to write
  • Better performance
  • Better scalability
  • Built-in async support

Q: Does every Task create a new Thread?

No.

Many Tasks use existing ThreadPool threads.

This is a common interview trick question.

Q: Which consumes more resources?

Thread.

Creating a new Thread is expensive.

Q: Can a Task return a value?

Yes.

Task<int> GetTotalAsync()

{

   return Task.FromResult(100);

}



Q: Can a Thread return a value directly?

No.

Additional mechanisms are required.

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: Why is Task preferred in ASP.NET Core?

Because ASP.NET Core applications handle many concurrent requests.

Creating Threads for every request would be expensive and reduce scalability.

Tasks efficiently utilize the ThreadPool and improve throughput.

21. Async/Await Deep Dive

Async and Await are keywords that simplify asynchronous programming in C#.

They allow long-running operations such as database calls, API requests, and file operations to execute without blocking the calling thread.

In ASP.NET Core, async/await improves scalability by freeing request threads while waiting for I/O operations.

Real Project Example

Database query:

public async Task<List<User>> GetUsersAsync()

{

   return await _context.Users.ToListAsync();

}

While waiting for SQL Server to respond, the thread is returned to the ThreadPool and can process other requests.

Follow-up Questions

Q: What does async do?

Marks a method as asynchronous.

public async Task GetDataAsync()

{

}



Q: What does await do?

Pauses execution until the asynchronous operation completes.

await GetDataAsync();



Q: Can we use await without async?

No.

Compiler error.

Q: Can we use async without await?

Yes.

But usually generates a warning.

Q: Does async create a new Thread?

No.

This is one of the most common interview questions.

Async is about non-blocking operations, not thread creation.

Q: What is the benefit of async in Web APIs?

Without async:

Request Thread

  ↓

Waits For Database

  ↓

Blocked

With async:

Request Thread

  ↓

Database Call Starts

  ↓

Thread Released

  ↓

Database Completes

  ↓

Thread Resumes

This improves scalability.

Q: What is an I/O Bound operation?

Operations waiting for external resources.

Examples:

  • Database Calls
  • API Calls
  • File Access

Async is highly beneficial here.

Q: What is a CPU Bound operation?

Operations performing intensive computation.

Examples:

  • Image Processing
  • Encryption
  • Large Calculations

Async alone may not improve performance here.

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: What happens internally when await is encountered?

  1. Method execution pauses.
  2. Current state is captured.
  3. Thread is released.
  4. Operation continues asynchronously.
  5. When completed, execution resumes from the await point.

This is implemented using a compiler-generated state machine.

22. ThreadPool

ThreadPool is a collection of reusable worker threads managed by the CLR.

Instead of creating and destroying Threads repeatedly, .NET reuses ThreadPool threads to improve performance and reduce resource consumption.

Most Tasks execute using ThreadPool threads.

Real Project Example

Task.Run(() =>

{

   ProcessData();

});

Internally:

Task

↓

ThreadPool

↓

Worker Thread

No new Thread is created.

Follow-up Questions

Q: Why use ThreadPool?

Benefits:

  • Better performance
  • Reduced memory usage
  • Thread reuse
  • Improved scalability

Q: What is the disadvantage of creating Threads manually?

  • Expensive
  • More memory
  • Increased context switching

Q: Can ThreadPool threads be reused?

Yes.

That is their primary purpose.

Q: Does ASP.NET Core use ThreadPool?

Yes.

ASP.NET Core heavily relies on ThreadPool threads.

Q: How can we queue work to ThreadPool?

ThreadPool.QueueUserWorkItem(

   state =>

   {

       Console.WriteLine("Work");

   });



23. Parallel Programming

Parallel Programming involves executing multiple operations simultaneously using multiple CPU cores to improve performance.

Unlike async programming, which focuses on non-blocking operations, parallel programming focuses on maximizing CPU utilization.

Real Project Example

Processing 10,000 records.

Without Parallelism:

foreach(var record in records)

{

   Process(record);

}



With Parallelism:

Parallel.ForEach(records,

   record =>

   {

       Process(record);

   });

Multiple CPU cores process records simultaneously.

Follow-up Questions

Q: Difference between Async and Parallel Programming?

Async:

I/O Bound

Parallel:

CPU Bound



Q: What is Parallel.ForEach?

Processes collection items concurrently.

Parallel.ForEach(items, item =>

{

});



Q: What are the risks of Parallel Programming?

  • Race Conditions
  • Deadlocks
  • Synchronization Issues

Q: When should Parallel Programming be used?

CPU-intensive work:

  • Data Processing
  • Image Processing
  • Scientific Calculations

Q: Should Parallel.ForEach be used for database calls?

Generally No.

Database calls are I/O bound.

Async/Await is preferred.

24. CancellationToken

CancellationToken provides a cooperative way to cancel ongoing asynchronous operations.

It allows applications to stop unnecessary work and free resources when operations are no longer needed.

Real Project Example

API request cancelled by user.

public async Task GetDataAsync(

   CancellationToken token)

{

   await Task.Delay(10000, token);

}

If the client disconnects, the operation can be cancelled.

Follow-up Questions

Q: Why use CancellationToken?

To:

  • Save resources
  • Improve responsiveness
  • Stop unnecessary processing

Q: How do we create one?

CancellationTokenSource cts =

   new CancellationTokenSource();



Q: How do we cancel?

cts.Cancel();



Q: How do we check cancellation?

token.ThrowIfCancellationRequested();



Q: Is cancellation forced?

No.

CancellationToken uses cooperative cancellation.

The code must respect the token.

25. ConfigureAwait

ConfigureAwait controls whether an awaited operation should attempt to resume on the original synchronization context after completion.

In ASP.NET Core, there is generally no synchronization context, so ConfigureAwait(false) usually provides little benefit compared to older ASP.NET Framework applications.

Real Project Example

await GetDataAsync()

     .ConfigureAwait(false);

The continuation can execute on any available thread.

Follow-up Questions

Q: Why was ConfigureAwait(false) important in ASP.NET Framework?

ASP.NET Framework had a SynchronizationContext.

Resuming on the original context could cause:

  • Performance overhead
  • Deadlocks

Q: Is ConfigureAwait(false) required in ASP.NET Core?

Usually No.

ASP.NET Core does not use the same SynchronizationContext model.

Q: Where is ConfigureAwait(false) still useful?

Library code.

Libraries should not assume a specific synchronization context.

Q: Can ConfigureAwait(false) improve performance?

Slightly, in some scenarios, by avoiding context capture.

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: Why do many developers still use ConfigureAwait(false) everywhere?

Because it was a best practice in ASP.NET Framework.

However, in ASP.NET Core the benefits are much smaller, and many teams use it only in reusable library code.

topics.html:
ASP.NET Core Web API

  1. REST API Principles
  2. HTTP Methods
  3. HTTP Status Codes
  4. Content Negotiation
  5. Swagger/OpenAPI
  6. API Versioning
  7. Pagination
  8. Filtering & Sorting
  9. Global Exception Handling
  10. Rate Limiting

38. What is a REST API?

REST (Representational State Transfer) is an architectural style used for designing web services that communicate over HTTP.

A REST API exposes resources through URLs and uses standard HTTP methods such as GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE to perform operations on those resources.

REST APIs are stateless, meaning each request contains all the information needed to process it.

In my projects, I use ASP.NET Core Web APIs to expose business functionality that can be consumed by React applications, mobile apps, and third-party systems.

Real Project Example

User Resource:

GET /api/users

GET /api/users/1

POST /api/users

PUT /api/users/1

DELETE /api/users/1

Each URL represents a resource.

Follow-up Questions

Q: What are REST principles?

  • Client-Server Architecture
  • Stateless Communication
  • Uniform Interface
  • Cacheable Responses
  • Layered System

Q: Why are REST APIs stateless?

Because each request contains all required information.

Benefits:

  • Scalability
  • Reliability
  • Simpler Architecture

Q: What is a resource in REST?

Example:

User

Order

Product

Report

Represented through URLs.

Q: Why is REST popular?

  • Simple
  • Platform Independent
  • HTTP Based
  • Scalable

39. HTTP Methods (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE)

HTTP methods define the action that should be performed on a resource.

Each method has a specific purpose in REST APIs.

GET

Retrieve data.

GET /api/users/1

Example:

[HttpGet("{id}")]

public IActionResult GetUser(int id)

{

}



POST

Create a new resource.

POST /api/users

Example:

[HttpPost]

public IActionResult CreateUser(

   CreateUserRequest request)

{

}



PUT

Replace the entire resource.

PUT /api/users/1



PATCH

Partially update a resource.

PATCH /api/users/1



DELETE

Remove a resource.

DELETE /api/users/1



Follow-up Questions

Q: Difference between PUT and PATCH?

PUT:

Full Update

PATCH:

Partial Update

Example:

Current User:

{

 "name":"Ashutosh",

 "email":"ash@gmail.com"

}

PUT requires sending entire object.

PATCH may update only:

{

 "email":"new@gmail.com"

}



Q: Which methods are idempotent?

Idempotent means repeated requests produce the same result.

Idempotent:

GET

PUT

DELETE

Not necessarily idempotent:

POST



Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: Why should GET never modify data?

GET should be safe and cacheable.

Changing data in GET violates REST principles.

40. HTTP Status Codes

HTTP Status Codes indicate the outcome of a request.

They help clients understand whether a request succeeded or failed.

Common Status Codes

200 OK

Request successful.

return Ok(data);



201 Created

Resource created successfully.

return CreatedAtAction(...);



204 No Content

Request successful but no response body.

return NoContent();



400 Bad Request

Client sent invalid data.

return BadRequest();



401 Unauthorized

Authentication required.

403 Forbidden

User authenticated but lacks permission.

404 Not Found

Resource does not exist.

409 Conflict

Conflict occurred.

Example:

Duplicate email.

500 Internal Server Error

Unexpected server error.

Follow-up Questions

Q: Difference between 401 and 403?

401:

Not Authenticated

403:

Authenticated But Not Authorized



Q: When should 201 be returned?

After successful resource creation.

Q: When should 204 be returned?

Successful operation with no content.

Example:

DELETE



41. Content Negotiation

Content Negotiation is the process by which the client and server agree on the response format.

The client specifies supported formats through the Accept header.

ASP.NET Core automatically selects the appropriate formatter.

Real Project Example

Request:

Accept: application/json

Response:

{

 "id":1

}



Request:

Accept: application/xml

Response:

<User>

 <Id>1</Id>

</User>



Follow-up Questions

Q: What header controls Content Negotiation?

Accept



Q: What format is most common?

JSON



Q: Why is Content Negotiation useful?

Supports multiple client types.

42. Swagger / OpenAPI

Swagger is a tool that automatically generates interactive API documentation based on API definitions.

It allows developers to view endpoints, request models, response models, and test APIs directly from the browser.

Swagger improves API discoverability and reduces integration effort.

Real Project Example

Installation:

builder.Services.AddEndpointsApiExplorer();

builder.Services.AddSwaggerGen();

Pipeline:

app.UseSwagger();

app.UseSwaggerUI();



Follow-up Questions

Q: Why use Swagger?

Benefits:

  • API Documentation
  • API Testing
  • Team Collaboration

Q: What is OpenAPI?

OpenAPI is the specification.

Swagger is the tool that implements it.

Q: Can Swagger generate request models?

Yes.

It automatically documents DTOs and endpoints.

43. API Versioning

API Versioning allows multiple versions of an API to coexist without breaking existing clients.

As APIs evolve, versioning helps maintain backward compatibility.

Real Project Example

Version 1:

/api/v1/users

Version 2:

/api/v2/users

Controller:

[ApiVersion("1.0")]

[Route("api/v{version:apiVersion}/users")]

public class UsersController : ControllerBase

{

}



Follow-up Questions

Q: Why is API Versioning important?

Prevents breaking existing consumers.

Q: Common Versioning Approaches?

URL Versioning

/api/v1/users



Header Versioning

api-version: 1.0



Query String Versioning

/api/users?version=1



Q: Which approach is most common?

URL Versioning.

44. Pagination

Pagination divides large datasets into smaller chunks to improve performance and reduce response size.

Instead of returning thousands of records, APIs return a subset of records per request.

Real Project Example

Request:

GET /api/users?page=1&pageSize=20

Controller:

[HttpGet]

public async Task<IActionResult> GetUsers(

   int page = 1,

   int pageSize = 20)

{

}



Follow-up Questions

Q: Why use Pagination?

Benefits:

  • Better Performance
  • Lower Memory Usage
  • Faster Responses

Q: What is Skip and Take?

var users = await _context.Users

   .Skip((page - 1) * pageSize)

   .Take(pageSize)

   .ToListAsync();



Q: What is the problem with returning all records?

Large payloads and poor performance.

45. Filtering & Sorting

Filtering allows clients to retrieve only relevant data, while sorting controls the order of returned records.

These techniques improve API usability and reduce unnecessary data transfer.

Real Project Example

Filtering:

GET /api/users?isActive=true

Sorting:

GET /api/users?sortBy=name



LINQ Example

var users = _context.Users

   .Where(x => x.IsActive)

   .OrderBy(x => x.Name);



Follow-up Questions

Q: Why implement filtering?

To reduce unnecessary data retrieval.

Q: Why implement sorting?

To return data in meaningful order.

Q: Can filtering and pagination be combined?

Yes.

Most production APIs use:

Filtering

Sorting

Pagination

together.

46. Global Exception Handling

Global Exception Handling centralizes error handling across the application.

Instead of placing try-catch blocks in every controller, exceptions are handled in one location.

This improves maintainability and consistency.

Real Project Example

Program.cs

app.UseExceptionHandler("/error");

Custom Middleware:

public class ExceptionMiddleware

{

}



Follow-up Questions

Q: Why avoid try-catch in every controller?

Because it leads to duplicated code.

Q: Benefits of Global Exception Handling?

  • Centralized Logging
  • Consistent Responses
  • Cleaner Controllers

Q: What status code is typically returned?

500 Internal Server Error



Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: What should be logged during exception handling?

  • Exception Message
  • Stack Trace
  • Request Path
  • Correlation Id

47. Rate Limiting

Rate Limiting restricts how many requests a client can make within a specific time period.

It protects APIs from abuse, accidental overload, and denial-of-service scenarios.

Real Project Example

ASP.NET Core Rate Limiter:

builder.Services.AddRateLimiter(options =>

{

});

Example Policy:

100 Requests Per Minute



Follow-up Questions

Q: Why use Rate Limiting?

  • Prevent Abuse
  • Protect Resources
  • Improve Stability

Q: What happens when limit is exceeded?

API returns:

429 Too Many Requests



Q: Common Rate Limiting Strategies?

Fixed Window

100 Requests / Minute



Sliding Window

More flexible moving time window.

Token Bucket

Tokens are replenished over time.

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: Where is Rate Limiting commonly applied?

  • Public APIs
  • Authentication Endpoints
  • Payment APIs
  • Search Endpoints

topics.title: Authentication Authorization
topics.html:
Authentication & Authorization

  1. Authentication vs Authorization
  2. JWT Authentication
  3. JWT Token Structure
  4. Refresh Tokens
  5. Claims & Roles
  6. Policy-Based Authorization
  7. Authentication Middleware
  8. ASP.NET Core Identity
  9. OAuth 2.0
  10. OpenID Connect

65. Authentication vs Authorization

Authentication and Authorization are two fundamental security concepts used in ASP.NET Core applications.

Authentication answers the question:

Who are you?

Authorization answers the question:

What are you allowed to do?

Authentication verifies the identity of the user, while Authorization determines what resources that authenticated user can access.

In my projects, I typically use JWT Authentication to verify users and Role-Based or Policy-Based Authorization to control access to APIs.

Real Project Example

User logs in:

Username + Password

      ↓

Authentication

      ↓

JWT Token Issued

User accesses API:

JWT Token

     ↓

Authorization Check

     ↓

Access Granted/Denied



Follow-up Questions

Q: Can Authorization happen without Authentication?

No.

The system must know who the user is before checking permissions.

Q: Example of Authentication?

Login Screen



Q: Example of Authorization?

Admin Can Delete Users

Normal User Cannot



Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: Where are Authentication and Authorization implemented in ASP.NET Core?

app.UseAuthentication();

app.UseAuthorization();

Authentication must execute before Authorization.

66. JWT Authentication

JWT (JSON Web Token) is a compact, secure way to transmit user identity information between a client and server.

After successful login, the server generates a JWT token and sends it to the client.

The client includes the token in subsequent requests, allowing the API to verify the user's identity without maintaining server-side session state.

JWT is widely used because it supports stateless authentication and scales well in distributed systems.

Real Project Example

Login:

POST /api/auth/login

Response:

{

  "token":"eyJhbGciOi..."

}

Subsequent requests:

Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi...



JWT Configuration

builder.Services

   .AddAuthentication(

       JwtBearerDefaults.AuthenticationScheme)

   .AddJwtBearer(options =>

   {

       options.TokenValidationParameters =

           new TokenValidationParameters

           {

           };

   });



Follow-up Questions

Q: Why use JWT?

Benefits:

  • Stateless
  • Scalable
  • Secure
  • Cross-platform

Q: Where is JWT stored?

Common options:

  • HttpOnly Cookie
  • Local Storage
  • Session Storage

Q: What header carries JWT?

Authorization: Bearer Token



Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: Why is JWT preferred for Microservices?

Because each service can validate the token independently without shared session storage.

67. JWT Token Structure

A JWT consists of three parts separated by dots.

Header.Payload.Signature

Example:

xxxxx.yyyyy.zzzzz



Structure

Header

Contains metadata.

Example:

{

 "alg":"HS256",

 "typ":"JWT"

}



Payload

Contains claims.

Example:

{

 "sub":"123",

 "name":"Ashutosh",

 "role":"Admin"

}



Signature

Used to verify token integrity.

Generated using:

Header

+

Payload

+

Secret Key



Follow-up Questions

Q: Can JWT payload be decoded?

Yes.

JWT is encoded, not encrypted.

Q: Should sensitive information be stored in JWT?

No.

Anyone possessing the token can decode the payload.

Q: What protects JWT from tampering?

Signature validation.

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: If JWT payload is visible, why is it secure?

Because attackers cannot modify the payload without invalidating the signature.

68. Refresh Tokens

Refresh Tokens are long-lived tokens used to obtain new access tokens when the current JWT expires.

This improves security because access tokens can have short expiration times while allowing users to stay logged in.

Real Project Example

Access Token:

15 Minutes

Refresh Token:

7 Days

Flow:

Access Token Expires

       ↓

Refresh Token Sent

       ↓

New Access Token Generated



Follow-up Questions

Q: Why not create long-lived JWTs?

Security risk.

If stolen, attackers retain access longer.

Q: Where should Refresh Tokens be stored?

Typically:

Database

HttpOnly Cookie



Q: Can Refresh Tokens be revoked?

Yes.

This is one of their biggest advantages.

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: What happens if a Refresh Token is compromised?

It should be revoked immediately and the user should be required to log in again.

69. Claims & Roles

Claims are pieces of information about a user stored inside the authentication token.

Roles are a specific type of claim used for authorization decisions.

Claims provide user identity and metadata, while roles determine permissions.

Real Project Example

Claims:

{

  "UserId":"1",

  "Email":"user@test.com",

  "Role":"Admin"

}



Role-Based Authorization

[Authorize(Roles = "Admin")]

public IActionResult DeleteUser()

{

   return Ok();

}

Only Admin users can access the endpoint.

Follow-up Questions

Q: What is a Claim?

User-related information.

Examples:

  • UserId
  • Email
  • Role

Q: What is a Role?

A permission grouping.

Examples:

Admin

Manager

User



Q: Where are Claims stored?

Typically inside JWT tokens.

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: Claims vs Roles?

Role:

High-Level Permission

Claim:

Any User Information

Claims provide greater flexibility.

70. Policy-Based Authorization

Policy-Based Authorization is a more flexible authorization approach than role-based authorization.

Instead of checking only roles, policies evaluate requirements and claims.

This is preferred for complex business rules.

Real Project Example

Policy Registration:

builder.Services.AddAuthorization(options =>

{

   options.AddPolicy(

       "EmployeeOnly",

       policy =>

       {

           policy.RequireClaim(

               "Department",

               "IT");

       });

});

Usage:

[Authorize(Policy = "EmployeeOnly")]

public IActionResult GetEmployeeData()

{

   return Ok();

}



Follow-up Questions

Q: Why use Policies instead of Roles?

Policies support more complex rules.

Q: Can Policies check Claims?

Yes.

That is one of their primary purposes.

Q: Can Policies combine multiple requirements?

Yes.

Multiple conditions can be evaluated.

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: When should Policy-Based Authorization be preferred?

When authorization depends on:

  • Department
  • Region
  • Subscription Level
  • Business Rules

rather than simple roles.

71. Authentication Middleware

Authentication Middleware validates incoming credentials and establishes the user identity for the current request.

Without Authentication Middleware, authorization cannot function correctly.

Real Project Example

app.UseAuthentication();

app.UseAuthorization();

Request Flow:

Request

   ↓

Authentication

   ↓

User Identity Created

   ↓

Authorization

   ↓

Controller



Follow-up Questions

Q: Why must Authentication run before Authorization?

Because Authorization requires an authenticated user.

Q: What happens if UseAuthorization comes first?

Authorization will fail because no user identity exists yet.

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: What does Authentication Middleware create?

A:

HttpContext.User

object containing Claims and Identity information.

72. ASP.NET Core Identity

ASP.NET Core Identity is Microsoft's membership and authentication framework.

It provides built-in functionality for:

  • User Management
  • Password Hashing
  • Login
  • Registration
  • Roles
  • Claims
  • Token Generation

Instead of building authentication from scratch, Identity provides a secure and tested implementation.

Real Project Example

Register Identity:

builder.Services

   .AddIdentity<ApplicationUser,

                IdentityRole>()

   .AddEntityFrameworkStores<AppDbContext>();



Follow-up Questions

Q: What problems does Identity solve?

  • User Storage
  • Password Security
  • Role Management
  • Authentication

Q: Does Identity hash passwords?

Yes.

Passwords should never be stored as plain text.

Q: Can Identity be used with JWT?

Yes.

Very common in production systems.

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: Why use Identity instead of creating custom authentication?

Because security implementations are difficult to get right and Identity already handles many security concerns.

73. OAuth 2.0

OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework that allows applications to access resources on behalf of a user without exposing the user's password.

It is commonly used for third-party login and delegated access.

Real Project Example

Login with:

  • Google
  • Microsoft
  • Facebook

Flow:

User

  ↓

Google Login

  ↓

Google Authorizes

  ↓

Access Token Issued



Follow-up Questions

Q: What problem does OAuth solve?

Delegated authorization.

Q: Does OAuth authenticate users?

OAuth primarily handles authorization.

Authentication is usually handled through OpenID Connect.

Q: Example of OAuth usage?

Login with Google



Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: Why not simply ask users for their Google password?

Security risk.

OAuth allows secure delegated access.

74. OpenID Connect (OIDC)

OpenID Connect is an identity layer built on top of OAuth 2.0.

OAuth tells applications what users can access.

OpenID Connect tells applications who the user is.

It is widely used for Single Sign-On (SSO).

Real Project Example

Login Flow:

User

 ↓

Google Login

 ↓

OAuth Authorization

 ↓

OpenID Connect Identity Token

 ↓

Application Receives User Information



Follow-up Questions

Q: Difference between OAuth and OpenID Connect?

OAuth:

Authorization

OpenID Connect:

Authentication



Q: What token does OpenID Connect introduce?

ID Token

Contains user identity information.

Q: What is SSO?

Single Sign-On.

One login provides access to multiple applications.

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: Why do modern enterprise applications use OpenID Connect?

Because it provides:

  • Secure Authentication
  • SSO Support
  • Standardized Identity Management
  • Integration with providers like Google, Microsoft, and enterprise identity platforms
