75. SOLID Principles

SOLID is a set of five object-oriented design principles that help create maintainable, scalable, and loosely coupled software.

The five principles are:

  • Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)
  • Open/Closed Principle (OCP)
  • Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)
  • Interface Segregation Principle (ISP)
  • Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP)

In enterprise applications, SOLID principles improve code readability, testability, and long-term maintainability.

Real Project Example

Instead of creating one large service that handles:

Validation

Database Access

Email Sending

Logging

we separate responsibilities into dedicated classes.

This follows SRP and makes the code easier to maintain.

Follow-up Questions

Q: Why are SOLID principles important?

Benefits:

  • Loose Coupling
  • Easier Testing
  • Better Maintainability
  • Easier Extension

Q: Which SOLID principle is used most often?

Typically:

SRP

DIP

because they directly influence everyday coding.

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: Does following SOLID guarantee good architecture?

No.

SOLID helps improve design but must be applied appropriately.

Overengineering can be as harmful as poor design.

76. Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)

A class should have only one reason to change.

In other words, a class should have only one responsibility.

Bad Example

public class UserService

{

   public void SaveUser()

   {

   }

   public void SendEmail()

   {

   }

   public void GenerateReport()

   {

   }

}

Multiple responsibilities.

Better Example

public class UserService

{

   public void SaveUser()

   {

   }

}



public class EmailService

{

   public void SendEmail()

   {

   }

}



Follow-up Questions

Q: Benefits of SRP?

  • Easier Testing
  • Easier Maintenance
  • Reduced Coupling

Q: How do you identify SRP violations?

Ask:

Does this class have multiple reasons to change?

If yes, SRP is likely violated.

77. Open/Closed Principle (OCP)

Software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification.

We should be able to add new functionality without changing existing working code.

Bad Example

if(paymentType == "CreditCard")

{

}

else if(paymentType == "PayPal")

{

}

Every new payment type requires modifying existing code.

Better Example

public interface IPaymentProcessor

{

   void Process();

}

Implementations:

CreditCardProcessor

PayPalProcessor

UPIProcessor

New processors can be added without modifying existing logic.

Follow-up Questions

Q: Which pattern commonly supports OCP?

Strategy Pattern.

Q: Why is OCP valuable?

Reduces risk of breaking existing functionality.

78. Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)

Derived classes should be replaceable with their base classes without changing application behavior.

If a subclass cannot properly fulfill the contract of its parent, LSP is violated.

Bad Example

public class Bird

{

   public virtual void Fly()

   {

   }

}



public class Penguin : Bird

{

   public override void Fly()

   {

       throw new Exception();

   }

}

Penguins cannot fly.

LSP violation.

Better Design

IFlyable

implemented only by birds that can fly.

Follow-up Questions

Q: Why is LSP important?

Ensures inheritance remains predictable.

Q: Common sign of LSP violation?

Methods throwing:

NotImplementedException

in derived classes.

79. Interface Segregation Principle (ISP)

Clients should not be forced to depend on interfaces they do not use.

Large interfaces should be split into smaller, focused interfaces.

Bad Example

public interface IWorker

{

   void Work();

   void Eat();

   void Sleep();

}

Not all implementations need every method.

Better Example

public interface IWorkable

{

   void Work();

}



public interface IEatable

{

   void Eat();

}



Follow-up Questions

Q: Why avoid large interfaces?

They create unnecessary dependencies.

Q: What is another name for ISP?

Fat Interface Prevention Principle.

80. Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP)

High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules.

Both should depend on abstractions.

This principle is the foundation of Dependency Injection.

Bad Example

public class UserService

{

   private SqlRepository _repo =

       new SqlRepository();

}

Tightly coupled.

Better Example

public class UserService

{

   private readonly IUserRepository _repo;

   public UserService(

       IUserRepository repo)

   {

       _repo = repo;

   }

}



Follow-up Questions

Q: How is DIP implemented in ASP.NET Core?

Using Dependency Injection.

Q: Why use abstractions?

Allows replacing implementations without changing consumers.

81. CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation)

CQRS separates read operations from write operations.

Commands modify data.

Queries retrieve data.

This separation improves scalability, maintainability, and performance.

Real Project Example

Command:

CreateUserCommand

Query:

GetUserByIdQuery



Structure

Controller

    ↓

Command

    ↓

Handler

and

Controller

    ↓

Query

    ↓

Handler



Follow-up Questions

Q: Benefits of CQRS?

  • Better Separation
  • Easier Scaling
  • Simpler Logic

Q: Should every application use CQRS?

No.

It adds complexity.

Best for medium-to-large systems.

82. Mediator Pattern

The Mediator Pattern reduces direct dependencies between components by introducing a mediator that coordinates communication.

In .NET, this is commonly implemented using the popular library MediatR.

Real Project Example

Without Mediator:

Controller

     ↓

Service

     ↓

Repository



With Mediator:

Controller

     ↓

Mediator

     ↓

Handler



Example

public record GetUserQuery(int Id);

Handler:

public class GetUserQueryHandler

{

}



Follow-up Questions

Q: Benefits of Mediator?

  • Loose Coupling
  • Cleaner Controllers
  • Easier Testing

Q: Does CQRS require MediatR?

No.

But they are commonly used together.

83. Factory Pattern

The Factory Pattern creates objects without exposing object creation logic to consumers.

Instead of using new directly, a factory decides which object to create.

Real Project Example

public interface IPaymentProcessor

{

}

Factory:

public class PaymentFactory

{

   public IPaymentProcessor Create(

       string paymentType)

   {

   }

}



Follow-up Questions

Q: Why use Factory Pattern?

  • Centralized Creation Logic
  • Reduced Coupling
  • Easier Extension

Q: Real-world examples?

Payment providers.

Credit Card

PayPal

UPI



84. Singleton Pattern

The Singleton Pattern ensures that only one instance of a class exists throughout the application's lifetime.

Example

public class CacheService

{

   private static readonly CacheService

       _instance =

       new CacheService();

   public static CacheService Instance

       => _instance;

}



ASP.NET Core Equivalent

builder.Services

   .AddSingleton<ICacheService,

                 CacheService>();



Follow-up Questions

Q: When should Singleton be used?

  • Cache Services
  • Configuration Services
  • Shared Utilities

Q: Risks of Singleton?

  • Global State
  • Thread Safety Issues

85. Strategy Pattern

The Strategy Pattern defines a family of algorithms and allows them to be swapped at runtime.

Instead of large if-else statements, behavior is selected dynamically.

Real Project Example

Payment Processing:

CreditCardStrategy

PayPalStrategy

UPIStrategy

Common interface:

IPaymentStrategy



Follow-up Questions

Q: Benefits?

  • Extensibility
  • Cleaner Code
  • Supports OCP

Q: Difference from Factory?

Factory:

Creates Objects

Strategy:

Changes Behavior



86. Microservices vs Monolith

A Monolithic architecture contains all functionality in a single deployable application.

A Microservices architecture breaks functionality into independently deployable services.

Monolith

UI

Business Logic

Database

Single deployment.

Microservices

User Service

Order Service

Payment Service

Separate deployments.

Follow-up Questions

Q: Advantages of Monolith?

  • Simpler Development
  • Easier Deployment
  • Easier Debugging

Q: Advantages of Microservices?

  • Independent Scaling
  • Independent Deployment
  • Better Team Ownership

Q: When choose Microservices?

Large systems with multiple teams and scaling requirements.

87. Clean Architecture

Clean Architecture organizes code into layers with dependencies pointing inward toward business rules.

The business layer remains independent of frameworks, databases, and UI technologies.

Layers

Presentation Layer

       ↓

Application Layer

       ↓

Domain Layer

       ↓

Infrastructure Layer



Real Project Example

API

↓

Application

↓

Domain

↓

Infrastructure

↓

SQL Server



Follow-up Questions

Q: Main benefit?

Business logic becomes independent of external technologies.

Q: Why is it popular?

  • Testability
  • Maintainability
  • Scalability

Senior-Level Follow-up

Q: Which layer contains business rules?

Domain Layer.

88. Onion Architecture

Onion Architecture is similar to Clean Architecture and organizes the application into concentric layers.

Dependencies always point inward.

The core business logic sits at the center.

Layers

Infrastructure

     ↓

Application

     ↓

Domain

Domain is the center.

Real Project Example

API

↓

Services

↓

Domain

↓

Repositories

↓

Database



Follow-up Questions

Q: Difference between Onion and Clean Architecture?

Both share similar goals:

  • Separation of Concerns
  • Dependency Rule
  • Testability

Clean Architecture is generally broader and more commonly referenced in modern .NET projects.

Q: Why keep Domain Layer independent?

Business rules should survive technology changes.

For example:

SQL Server → PostgreSQL

React → Angular

REST → GraphQL

without changing core business logic.

class="c4">IOptionsMonitor:</span></p><p class="c1"><span class="c6"></span><span class="c8 c6">Supports Runtime Changes</span></p><p class="c1"><span class="c6"></span><hr></p><h1 class="c14" id="h.533b8xxi80y3"><span class="c11 c15">122. Global Exception Handling Middleware</span></h1><h2 class="c9" id="h.z2hwspnwz2dq"></h2><p class="c1"><span class="c4">Global Exception Handling Middleware centralizes exception handling for the entire application.</span></p><p class="c1"><span class="c4">Instead of writing try-catch blocks everywhere, exceptions are handled in one place.</span></p><hr><p class="c1 c2"><span class="c4"></span></p><h2 class="c9" id="h.564bs5lzen9s"><span class="c3">Real Project Example</span></h2><p class="c1"><span class="c7 c6"></span><span class="c8 c6">app.UseExceptionHandler(</span></p><p class="c1"><span class="c8 c6">   "/error");</span></p><p class="c1"><span class="c6"></span><span class="c4">Custom Middleware:</span></p><p class="c1"><span class="c6"></span><span class="c8 c6">try</span></p><p class="c1"><span class="c8 c6">{</span></p><p class="c1"><span class="c8 c6">   await _next(context);</span></p><p class="c1"><span class="c8 c6">}</span></p><p class="c1"><span class="c8 c6">catch(Exception ex)</span></p><p class="c1"><span class="c8 c6">{</span></p><p class="c1"><span class="c8 c6">   _logger.LogError(ex,</span></p><p class="c1"><span class="c8 c6">       "Unhandled Exception");</span></p><p class="c1"><span class="c8 c6">}</span></p><p class="c1"><span class="c6"></span><hr></p><h2 class="c9" id="h.enb5u2ckcfq0"><span class="c3">Follow-up Questions</span></h2><h3 class="c0" id="h.lbpkaxitgap4"><span class="c11 c10">Q: Benefits?</span></h3><ul class="c12 lst-kix_qgyeywx4r0yt-0 start"><li class="c1 c5 li-bullet-0"><span class="c4">Cleaner Controllers</span></li><li class="c1 c5 li-bullet-0"><span class="c4">Centralized Logging</span></li><li class="c1 c5 li-bullet-0"><span class="c4">Consistent Responses</span></li></ul><hr><p class="c1 c2"><span class="c4"></span></p><h3 class="c0" id="h.su14uidnygll"><span class="c11 c10">Q: What status code is usually returned?</span></h3><p class="c1"><span class="c10 c6"></span><span class="c8 c6">500 Internal Server Error</span></p><p class="c1"><span class="c6"></span><hr></p><h3 class="c0" id="h.xq1tupvn2vfr"><span class="c10 c11">Senior-Level Follow-up</span></h3><h3 class="c0" id="h.y0pbgp2gmxl"><span class="c11 c10">Q: What should be logged?</span></h3><ul class="c12 lst-kix_823nrh2rii3-0 start"><li class="c1 c5 li-bullet-0"><span class="c4">Message</span></li><li class="c1 c5 li-bullet-0"><span class="c4">Stack Trace</span></li><li class="c1 c5 li-bullet-0"><span class="c4">Request Path</span></li><li class="c1 c5 li-bullet-0"><span class="c4">Correlation ID</span></li></ul><hr><p class="c1 c2"><span class="c4"></span></p><h1 class="c14" id="h.o1did56eczds"><span class="c11 c15">123. Correlation ID</span></h1><h2 class="c9" id="h.nmxtswinj6bu"></h2><p class="c1"><span class="c4">A Correlation ID is a unique identifier attached to a request that allows tracking the request across multiple services and logs.</span></p><p class="c1"><span class="c4">It is extremely useful in distributed systems and microservices.</span></p><hr><p class="c1 c2"><span class="c4"></span></p><h2 class="c9" id="h.27r6ay1h28zt"><span class="c3">Real Project Example</span></h2><p class="c1"><span class="c7 c6"></span><span class="c8 c6">Request</span></p><p class="c1"><span class="c8 c6"> ↓</span></p><p class="c1"><span class="c8 c6">Correlation ID:</span></p><p class="c1"><span class="c8 c6">ABC123</span></p><p class="c1"><span class="c6"></span><span class="c4">Logs:</span></p><p class="c1"><span class="c6"></span><span class="c8 c6">ABC123 - API Received</span></p><p class="c1 c2"><span class="c8 c6"></span></p><p class="c1"><span class="c8 c6">ABC123 - Database Query</span></p><p class="c1 c2"><span class="c8 c6"></span></p><p class="c1"><span class="c8 c6">ABC123 - Response Sent</span></p><p class="c1"><span class="c6"></span><hr></p><h2 class="c9" id="h.26ghxgul21es"><span class="c3">Follow-up Questions</span></h2><h3 class="c0" id="h.6w02t4qy9bts"><span class="c11 c10">Q: Why use Correlation IDs?</span></h3><p class="c1"><span class="c4">To trace requests across systems.</span></p><hr><p class="c1 c2"><span class="c4"></span></p><h3 class="c0" id="h.a34q1y3jelzf"><span class="c11 c10">Q: Where are Correlation IDs stored?</span></h3><p class="c1"><span class="c4">Typically:</span></p><p class="c1"><span class="c6"></span><span class="c8 c6">X-Correlation-ID</span></p><p class="c1"><span class="c6"></span><span class="c4">header.</span></p><hr><p class="c1 c2"><span class="c4"></span></p><h3 class="c0" id="h.39f05p5dq24u"><span class="c11 c10">Senior-Level Follow-up</span></h3><h3 class="c0" id="h.nagsr1wbezqo"><span class="c11 c10">Q: Why are Correlation IDs critical in Microservices?</span></h3><p class="c1"><span class="c4">Because a single request may travel through many services and logs.</span></p><p class="c1 c2"><span class="c4"></span></p><p class="c2 c16"><span class="c4"></span></p></body></html>

topics.title: Follow-up Questions
topics.html:
1. Why is String Immutable?

String is immutable because once a string object is created, its value cannot be changed.

Whenever a modification occurs, .NET creates a new string object instead of modifying the existing one.

This design improves:

  • Thread Safety
  • Security
  • Hashing Performance
  • String Interning

Follow-up

Q: Then why doesn't this modify the string?

string name = "John";

name += " Smith";

Answer

Because a new string object is created:

"John"

  ↓

"John Smith"

The original string remains unchanged.

Q: When should StringBuilder be used?

When performing multiple string modifications inside loops.

2. Why is StringBuilder Faster?

StringBuilder is mutable.

Instead of creating new objects repeatedly, it modifies an internal buffer.

Follow-up

Q: Is StringBuilder always faster?

No.

For small string operations:

string fullName = first + last;

String is usually fine.

StringBuilder becomes beneficial when many modifications occur.

3. Why is DbContext Scoped?

DbContext is designed to represent a single unit of work per request.

ASP.NET Core registers DbContext as Scoped by default.

Follow-up

Q: Why not Singleton?

Because DbContext is not thread-safe.

Multiple requests sharing the same instance can cause:

  • Data Corruption
  • Concurrency Issues
  • Unexpected Behavior

Q: Why not Transient?

Multiple repositories may receive different DbContext instances within the same request.

This can cause tracking issues.

4. Why is Repository Pattern Sometimes Avoided?

Repository Pattern was originally designed to abstract data access.

However, Entity Framework already implements:

  • Repository Pattern
  • Unit of Work Pattern

Follow-up

Q: Is Repository Pattern always needed with EF Core?

No.

Many modern applications use DbContext directly.

Q: When is Repository useful?

When:

  • Multiple Data Sources Exist
  • Complex Business Rules Exist
  • Testing Requires Abstraction

5. Why Use async/await?

Async/await improves scalability by preventing threads from being blocked during I/O operations.

Follow-up

Q: Does async make code faster?

No.

It improves scalability, not execution speed.

Q: Example?

Database call:

await _context.Users.ToListAsync();

Thread becomes available while waiting.

6. What Happens Internally When Await Is Encountered?

When await is reached:

  1. Method pauses
  2. Thread is released
  3. Operation continues in background
  4. Method resumes when completed

Follow-up

Q: Does await create a new thread?

No.

This is a very common misconception.

7. Task vs Thread?

Task is an abstraction over asynchronous work.

Thread is an OS-level execution unit.

Follow-up

Q: Does every Task create a Thread?

No.

Tasks often use the Thread Pool.

Q: Which should be preferred?

Task.

8. Why Is Any() Better Than Count()?

Any() stops as soon as a matching record is found.

Count() counts all records.

Follow-up

Q: SQL Generated?

Any():

EXISTS(...)

Count():

COUNT(*)

EXISTS is generally more efficient.

9. FirstOrDefault vs SingleOrDefault

FirstOrDefault returns first match.

SingleOrDefault expects exactly one match.

Follow-up

Q: Which should be used for Email?

SingleOrDefault

Because Email should be unique.

Q: What if duplicates exist?

SingleOrDefault throws exception.

10. Why Dependency Injection?

Dependency Injection promotes loose coupling and testability.

Follow-up

Q: What problem does it solve?

Without DI:

new SqlRepository();

Hard dependency.

With DI:

IUserRepository

Flexible dependency.

11. Why Constructor Injection?

Constructor Injection makes dependencies explicit and mandatory.

Follow-up

Q: Why not Property Injection?

Object can be created in invalid state.

Dependencies may be missing.

12. Why Middleware Instead Of Writing Logic In Controllers?

Middleware handles cross-cutting concerns.

Examples:

  • Logging
  • Authentication
  • Exception Handling

Follow-up

Q: Benefits?

Avoids duplicate code.

13. Why Authentication Before Authorization?

Authorization requires an authenticated identity.

Follow-up

Q: What happens if order is reversed?

Authorization fails because no user exists yet.

14. Why JWT Instead Of Session?

JWT is stateless.

No server-side session storage required.

Follow-up

Q: Why useful for Microservices?

Every service can validate token independently.

15. Why Refresh Tokens?

Refresh Tokens allow short-lived access tokens while maintaining user sessions.

Follow-up

Q: Why not long-lived JWT?

Security risk if token is stolen.

16. Why Use Redis?

Redis provides distributed caching across multiple servers.

Follow-up

Q: Why not Memory Cache?

Memory Cache exists only inside one server.

17. Why Use RabbitMQ?

RabbitMQ enables asynchronous communication.

Follow-up

Q: Why not direct API calls?

Direct calls create tight coupling.

Queues improve reliability.

18. Why Use CQRS?

CQRS separates read and write responsibilities.

Follow-up

Q: Should every application use CQRS?

No.

It adds complexity.

Use when benefits outweigh costs.

19. Why Use MediatR?

MediatR reduces coupling between Controllers and Business Logic.

Follow-up

Q: Is MediatR mandatory for CQRS?

No.

CQRS can exist without MediatR.

20. Why Use Clean Architecture?

Clean Architecture keeps business logic independent of frameworks.

Follow-up

Q: Biggest Advantage?

Technology changes do not impact core business rules.

21. Why Is EF Core Tracking Expensive?

EF Core stores entity state information to detect changes.

Tracking consumes memory and CPU.

Follow-up

Q: How improve performance?

.AsNoTracking()

for read-only queries.

22. Why Use Pagination?

Pagination prevents loading large datasets into memory.

Follow-up

Q: Example?

Bad:

Users.ToList()

Good:

Users.Skip(0)

    .Take(50)



23. Why Use Health Checks?

Health Checks allow monitoring systems to determine application health.

Follow-up

Q: Who consumes health endpoints?

  • Kubernetes
  • Load Balancers
  • Monitoring Tools

24. Why Use Docker?

Docker ensures applications run consistently across environments.

Follow-up

Q: Main advantage?

Works on my machine

problem disappears.

25. Why Use Kubernetes?

Kubernetes automates deployment, scaling, and recovery.

Follow-up

Q: What happens if a container crashes?

Kubernetes automatically recreates it.

26. Why Use SignalR?

SignalR provides real-time communication.

Follow-up

Q: Examples?

  • Chat
  • Notifications
  • Live Dashboards

27. Why Use gRPC?

gRPC provides high-performance communication between services.

Follow-up

Q: Why Faster Than REST?

Protocol Buffers are smaller than JSON.

28. Why Use Caching?

Caching reduces expensive operations.

Follow-up

Q: What should be cached?

  • Frequently Read Data
  • Rarely Changing Data

29. Why Is Singleton Dangerous?

Singletons create shared state.

Follow-up

Q: Main risk?

Thread safety issues.

30. Why Use ILogger Instead Of Console.WriteLine?

ILogger supports:

  • Log Levels
  • Structured Logging
  • Multiple Providers

Follow-up

Q: Production use?

ILogger or Serilog.

Never Console.WriteLine.

API Suddenly Becomes Slow in Production</span></h1><h2 class="c5" id="h.uwcq8nd112pb"><span class="c4">Interview Question</span></h2><p class="c11"><span class="c3">Your API response time increased from 200ms to 10 seconds in production. How would you investigate?</span></p><hr><p class="c2 c10"><span class="c3"></span></p><h2 class="c5" id="h.xkhlxeze7uxi"></h2><p class="c11"><span class="c3">I would follow a structured approach instead of making assumptions.</span></p><p class="c11"><span class="c3">First, I would identify whether the bottleneck is in:</span></p><ul class="c8 lst-kix_kpy28ngd0bqd-0 start"><li class="c6 li-bullet-0"><span class="c3">Database</span></li><li class="c6 li-bullet-0"><span class="c3">External APIs</span></li><li class="c6 li-bullet-0"><span class="c3">Application Code</span></li><li class="c6 li-bullet-0"><span class="c3">Infrastructure</span></li><li class="c6 li-bullet-0"><span class="c3">Network</span></li></ul><p class="c11"><span class="c3">I would check logs, monitoring dashboards, SQL query performance, CPU usage, memory consumption, and recent deployments.</span></p><hr><p class="c2 c10"><span class="c3"></span></p><h2 class="c5" id="h.9rc3hc5rntd7"><span class="c4">Investigation Steps</span></h2><p class="c2"><span class="c1"></span><span class="c9 c7">Application Insights</span></p><p class="c2"><span class="c9 c7">       ↓</span></p><p class="c0">Q: Most common cause?</span></h3><p class="c11"><span class="c3">Slow database queries.</span></p><hr><p class="c2 c10"><span class="c3"></span></p><h1 class="c12" id="h.pn950980sczy"><span class="c13">2. Memory Usage Keeps Increasing</span></h1><h2 class="c5" id="h.h3tc9ovnfcc7"><span class="c4">Interview Question</span></h2><p class="c11"><span class="c3">Application memory keeps increasing every day until restart.
